query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Low-temperature annealing of a non-equilibrium MgAlCuZnGd high-entropy alloy drives selective nanoscale segregation and grain-boundary precipitation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases, which in turn modify local electrochemical interactions and oxide scale nucleation, leading to altered corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behaviors relative to the as-quenched state.
generation.material_initial_state: An induction‐melted, as-quenched MgAlCuZnGd high-entropy alloy exhibiting a metastable solid solution with minor, dispersed intermetallic phases.
generation.intervention: Controlled low-temperature annealing at 300 °C for 5 hours in an inert atmosphere, with pre- and post-treatment high-resolution (e.g., TEM and APT) microstructural characterization.
generation.conditions: Annealing in an inert (Ar) atmosphere at 300 °C for 5 hours vs. a rapidly quenched baseline; alloy density maintained below 6 g/cm³ and compositional complexity preserved.
generation.structural_mediator: Development and spatial redistribution of nanoscale Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries via selective elemental segregation.
generation.mechanism: The low-temperature annealing promotes element partitioning within the metastable matrix, leading to the formation of intermetallic networks. These networks alter local microgalvanic coupling and serve as preferential sites for oxide scale nucleation during high-temperature exposure, thereby modifying the kinetics and morphology of oxidation and facilitating localized accelerated corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed samples will exhibit increased localized corrosion rates and changes in high-temperature oxidation behavior, such as the development of thicker yet less adherent oxide layers, compared to the as-quenched baseline.
generation.baseline: Rapidly quenched, as-processed MgAlCuZnGd alloy with minimal intermetallic segregation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to the induction‐melted MgAlCuZnGd alloy system under conditions where the density remains below 6 g/cm³ and within the set annealing temperature/time regime; effects are expected to be observable within these processing limits.
generation.uncertainty: The uniformity and extent of nanoscale segregation and its direct quantitative impact on microgalvanic activity and oxide scale properties remain uncertain until detailed characterization is performed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical MgAlCuZnGd alloy samples; subject half to the 300 °C/5-hour annealing treatment (with inert atmosphere) and retain the other half as rapidly quenched controls. Perform comprehensive microstructural characterization (TEM, APT) to assess intermetallic distribution, and conduct electrochemical corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization and EIS) along with high-temperature oxidation tests under identical conditions.
measurements: Nanoscale distribution and composition of intermetallic precipitates
Corrosion rates and electrochemical behavior (PDP curves, EIS parameters)
Oxide scale thickness, morphology, and adhesion metrics via SEM/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant increase in localized corrosion rates or any distinct change in oxide scale morphology (i.e., if intermetallic segregation levels and functional properties remain similar to the as-quenched baseline), then the hypothesized mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The PDP curves revealed that both the 4TZ and TZ alloys were more corrosion resistant than pure Mg. Both PDP and optical microscopy during immersion tests indicated that TZ was more corrosion resistant than the 4TZ alloy. The presence of Ti2Zn in the TZ alloys could be attributed to the increased corrosion resistance. Şuctic et al. demonstrated that Ti rich intermetallics in Zn alloys act as corrosion barriers, stabilizing the surrounding matrix []. Similarly, Ti2Zn may have helped stabilize the Mg matrix by acting as a barrier, probably forming inert islands of TiOx, slowing the propagation of corrosion fronts, while also promoting localized anodic dissolution of Mg due to galvanic interactions. This localized effect, along with the distribution of Ti rich phases around micropores, may have created cathodic sites, leading to variations in corrosion susceptibility across the alloy.

The properties for the elements that enter the calculations were acquired from valuable sources, suggested by the authors that originally developed the criteria, such as: atomic radius [], Allen electronegativity [,], melting temperatures [], and pair mixing enthalpy []. The optimization of the alloy compositions was performed by means of the multi-objective optimization module from MATLAB software (version 6.02, MatCalc Engineering GmbH, Vienna, Austria). MatCalc Pro edition, version 6.02, was used for multi-component phase equilibrium and thermodynamics by CALPHAD method, as well as non-equilibrium solidification and multi-phase precipitation kinetics. The optimal alloy compositions were prepared in an induction furnace type Linn MFG-30 (Linn High Therm GmbH, Eschenfelden, Germany) with inert atmosphere and cast in a copper mould. Technical purity raw materials of Al, Cu, Si, Zn, Mg, and Mn were used in the experimental trials. A 350 g charge for each alloy was placed in an alumina-based crucible. The alloys were melted in the induction furnace and cast in a copper mould, under protective atmosphere. The resulted as-cast alloys were annealed in an electrical furnace, LHT 04/17 Na

proposals.material_system: MgAlCuZnGd high-entropy alloy (non-equilibrium induction‐melted state, density <6 g/cm³)
proposals.intervention: Perform a controlled low-temperature annealing treatment (e.g., 250–350 °C for several hours) on as-quenched samples
proposals.conditions: Annealing in an inert atmosphere (Ar or N₂) at 300 °C for 5 hours compared with a rapidly quenched baseline
proposals.structural_mediator: Nanoscale segregation and formation of grain-boundary intermetallic precipitates (e.g., Mg-rich phases)
proposals.mechanism: The treatment is expected to drive selective element partitioning in the metastable solid solution. The resulting network of Mg-enriched intermetallics at the grain boundaries forms microgalvanic cells that locally accelerate anodic dissolution (enhancing corrosion in certain sites) and simultaneously modify the nucleation/growth of protective oxide scales during high-temperature exposure.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-quenched baseline, the annealed alloy should show increased localized corrosion rates (due to galvanic effects) and altered high-temperature oxidation behavior, such as less adherent but possibly thicker oxide scales owing to intermetallic‐induced disruptions.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This hypothesis links the non-equilibrium initial state, its controlled thermal evolution (via annealing), and the resulting microstructural reorganization (segregation at boundaries) to changes in corrosion and high-temperature oxidation performance, addressing how metastable transformations alter functional properties.

proposals.material_system: AlMgₓTiSnZn alloy system modified to include Mg (density <6 g/cm³, produced by rapid solidification)
proposals.intervention: Employ varying cooling rates (rapid quenching vs. moderate cooling) after melt processing to control the initial extent of solute trapping
proposals.conditions: Two processing routes: one with melt spinning (very high cooling rate) and one with induction melting followed by slow air cooling, with subsequent identical isothermal aging at 300 °C for 3 hours
proposals.structural_mediator: Retention versus nucleation of metastable supersaturated solid solution and subsequent precipitation of intermetallic phases
proposals.mechanism: A higher cooling rate maintains a homogeneously metastable state while slower cooling allows partial equilibrium and early-stage precipitation. The aging treatment then drives further transformation in both cases, though at different extents. These microstructural evolutions are expected to influence the corrosion behavior by altering localized electrochemical differences and modify the kinetics and morphology of high-temperature oxide film formation.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Rapidly quenched samples would form a fine, uniformly distributed precipitate structure during aging leading to relatively improved corrosion resistance and more uniform, adherent oxide scales, while the slowly cooled baseline would show coarser, inhomogeneous precipitates with poorer corrosion and oxidation behavior.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach directly investigates how the initial non-equilibrium processing (via cooling rate) influences the subsequent transformation pathways and functional properties, providing a controlled comparison to test the mechanistic hypothesis regarding microstructural evolution.

proposals.material_system: MgAlCuZnGd lightweight high-entropy alloy fabricated by induction melting
proposals.intervention: Subject samples to cyclic thermal oxidation tests to accelerate the evolution from metastable to stable microstructures
proposals.conditions: Thermal cycling between room temperature and 700 °C in air (e.g., 100 cycles with 30-minute dwells at both temperatures) vs. an isothermal baseline at room temperature
proposals.structural_mediator: Transformation of metastable solute distributions into thermodynamically stable intermetallic clusters that influence the oxide scale formation
proposals.mechanism: Thermal cycling promotes repeated expansion and contraction along with oxidation/diffusion at the surface, triggering the coarsening and spatial redistribution of intermetallic compounds. This evolution alters the nucleation sites and growth kinetics for the oxide scale, which in turn changes the alloy’s corrosion resistance under ambient conditions. The cycling serves as an accelerated test of the transformation pathway of the metastable state.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Cycled samples should exhibit a distinct oxide layer morphology (e.g., thicker but less adherent scale) and increased corrosion rates compared to the baseline isothermally held specimens, as the redistribution of phases creates micro-environments that promote oxidation and corrosion.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It tests a mechanistic link by imposing a defined thermal history that drives phase evolution from metastable to more stable intermetallic microstructures, then correlates those changes with variations in corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior, offering a clear falsifiable comparison.

proposals.material_system: Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloy produced via additive manufacturing (AM)
proposals.intervention: Design and fabricate samples with graded Mg concentrations to locally control metastability and phase evolution, then perform site-specific corrosion and oxidation tests
proposals.conditions: AM processing with controlled layer-by-layer composition variation (e.g., Mg content varied from low to high across the sample) followed by a uniform post-process heat treatment at 350 °C for 2 hours in vacuum
proposals.structural_mediator: Local differences in solute concentration leading to variable formation of stable intermetallic compounds and in-situ oxide scale adhesion characteristics
proposals.mechanism: The graded composition results in spatially resolved differences in transformation kinetics from the initial metastable state to equilibrium phases. Regions with higher Mg content are expected to nucleate and grow intermetallic phases more rapidly, altering the local electrochemical potential and influencing both corrosion behavior and the development of protective oxide films under high-temperature exposure.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Regions with higher Mg and more rapid phase transformation are predicted to show poorer corrosion resistance and non-uniform, less adherent oxide layers compared to low Mg regions. A controlled comparison between the graded regions will validate the mechanistic role of local phase evolution.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach leverages composition gradients as a tunable parameter to systematically explore how non-equilibrium transformations affect corrosion and oxidization, thereby testing the hypothesis that variations in transformation pathways lead to predictable changes in functional properties under controlled boundary conditions.

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes. It directly tests how thermal cycling drives the transformation from a metastable state to stable intermetallic clusters that affect oxidation and corrosion behavior.
critiques.constraints: Yes. It uses the specified MgAlCuZnGd alloy produced by induction melting and respects the density (<6 g/cm³) and compositional complexity constraints.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism of thermal expansion–contraction and oxidation‐facilitated diffusion leading to intermetallic coarsening is physically plausible for such alloys, although its direct linkage to oxide nucleation/damage might be oversimplified.
critiques.feasibility: Yes. Thermal cycling experiments with controlled temperature dwell times are established and feasible with current methods.
critiques.evidence: Some supporting insights come from studies on phase separation and oxidation behavior in complex alloys (e.g., PMC12843182 and PMC6356250), though these records are for different alloy systems and may only indirectly support the mechanism.
critiques.main_risk: The cyclic oxidation test may not accurately replicate the natural transformation pathway seen during service, and the mechanism might conflate effects from thermal stress with those due solely to phase evolution.
critiques.fix: Include pre- and post-cycling microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM/SEM) to directly correlate intermetallic evolution with changes in oxide morphology and corrosion behavior.

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes. It leverages composition gradients to test the role of local metastability and phase evolution on corrosion and oxidation, directly linking non-equilibrium transformations to property variability.
critiques.constraints: Yes. The method uses the MgAlCuZnGd system produced by additive manufacturing which inherently satisfies the density and composition constraints while introducing controlled variation.
critiques.physical_soundness: The idea that localized differences in Mg content drive variable transformation kinetics is physically sound; however, AM processing may introduce additional microstructural heterogeneities that complicate interpretation.
critiques.feasibility: Yes. Additive manufacturing with layer-by-layer composition control and subsequent heat treatment is within current technological capabilities.
critiques.evidence: Supported by prior observations on graded compositions affecting corrosion resistance and oxide scale properties (e.g., PMC9102090 and PMC12299034), although these studies do not address the exact high-entropy alloy system.
critiques.main_risk: Potential confounding from AM-induced defects and other processing artifacts might obscure the specific effects of composition-driven phase evolution.
critiques.fix: Implement complementary controls (e.g., samples produced via traditional processing) to isolate the effects of graded composition from other AM-related microstructural defects.

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes. It investigates how differences in cooling rate influence the retention of a metastable state and subsequent phase evolution, thereby affecting corrosion and oxidation behaviors.
critiques.constraints: Yes. Although the alloy system here (AlMgₓTiSnZn) differs somewhat from MgAlCuZnGd, it still meets the density constraint (<6 g/cm³) and relates to prior studies on AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism of solute trapping versus early precipitation controlled by cooling rate is physically sound and common in non-equilibrium solidification processes.
critiques.feasibility: Yes. The use of rapid solidification (melt spinning) versus slower cooling is well established and followed by isothermal aging to accentuate differences.
critiques.evidence: The evidence from literature (such as PMC10056590) supports the impact of cooling rate on phase evolution and microstructural outcomes, which can be linked to variations in corrosion and oxidation behavior.
critiques.main_risk: Complex microstructural evolution may arise from both the processing differences and aging treatment, making it challenging to attribute property changes solely to the initial cooling rate differences.
critiques.fix: Incorporate in-situ or time-resolved microstructural characterization during aging to decouple the effects of cooling rate from those of subsequent phase precipitation.

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes. It links a controlled low-temperature annealing process to nanoscale segregation and intermetallic precipitation, which in turn is hypothesized to modify corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
critiques.constraints: Yes. The approach uses the designated MgAlCuZnGd high-entropy alloy and adheres to the density (<6 g/cm³) and processing conditions provided.
critiques.physical_soundness: The idea that low-temperature annealing drives grain-boundary segregation and consequent microgalvanic coupling is physically plausible, reflecting common metallurgical behavior in non-equilibrium alloys.
critiques.feasibility: Yes. Controlled annealing treatments are straightforward and can be precisely executed in inert atmospheres.
critiques.evidence: Supporting evidence from studies on similar systems (e.g., PMC7579168 and PMC12299034) indicate that controlled heat treatments affect intermetallic distributions and corrosion response in complex alloys.
critiques.main_risk: The low-temperature annealing might not induce significant or uniform segregation, leading to ambiguous correlations between microstructural changes and macroscopic corrosion/oxidation behavior.
critiques.fix: Enhance the approach by employing high-resolution mapping techniques (e.g., atom probe tomography) to confirm the formation and distribution of nanoscale intermetallics and directly correlate these with changes in functional properties.

decision.rationale: Direction D directly targets the open question by linking a controlled, low-temperature annealing treatment of an as-quenched MgAlCuZnGd high‐entropy alloy to a measurable evolution in microstructure (nanoscale segregation and intermetallic precipitation) that mediates changes in corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior. The critic’s comments note the risk that the annealing treatment might not induce sufficiently uniform segregation; this can be mitigated with high-resolution mapping (e.g., atom probe tomography). Overall, it offers a clearly defined controlled comparison between an annealed state and an as-quenched baseline under specified conditions.
